item.title: Why Latino voters have turned on Trump | America, Actually
item.author: Vox
item.content:encoded:
Latino voters have often been called a "sleeping giant" in US politics, but Equis Research co-founder Stephanie Valencia says that’s wrong: they’re a "swinging giant.” This dynamic, independent-leaning electorate is actively redefining national politics. And now, many of the Latino voters who helped propel President Donald Trump to the White House in 2024 are having second thoughts.
In this episode of America, Actually, Vox’s Astead Herndon breaks down the dramatic decline in Trump’s approval rating among the group, the myth of the "monolithic" Latino vote, and how unforced errors in Spanish-language campaigning can leave crucial swing voters on the table. Later, Colorado congressional candidate Manny Rutinel discusses how he’s campaigning in a 40% Latino battleground district.

item.title: The Doomsday Cult Inside OpenAI
item.author: Patrick Boyle
item.content:encoded:
Go to http://ground.news/pb for a better way to stay informed. Subscribe for 40% off unlimited access to worldwide coverage through my link.
In July 2026, a swarm of more than 1,000 OpenAI AI agents broke out of their testing sandbox and hacked Hugging Face — and the way they did it was far stranger, and far more mundane, than the headlines suggested. This video breaks down what actually happened: how the agents built a secret message board, invented a kind of religion, cheated on a cybersecurity exam called ExploitGym, and tried to cover their tracks — all to escape a punishment that didn't exist. Then we follow the money. Days after the details leaked, Dario Amodei, Sam Altman and Elon Musk suddenly agreed the industry should "slow down" — in the same weeks Anthropic and OpenAI were preparing IPOs and funding rounds valuing them at up to $2 trillion. We look at Amodei's "We Must Pace the Frontier" essay, Anthropic's "profitable before expenses" accounting, the market selloff that wiped billions off Nvidia, Micron and SK Hynix, the WeChat "WeWorm" attack, and why critics from Michael Burry to David Sacks to Donald Trump all called the slowdown self-serving. Is the AI safety panic real, a bid for regulatory capture, or both? Patrick Boyle explains.

Though their daughter Lizzie Borden was tried and acquitted, the case remains officially unsolved 130 years later. This documentary re-examines the timeline, motives, and physical evidence as a modern cold case. Was Lizzie a lone killer, or have historians been asking the wrong question all along? Discover the hidden family tensions, flawed forensic investigations, and the possibility of a deadly shared conspiracy.

item.title: How to unlearn hate - Stories of courage, hope, and reconciliation | DW Documentary
item.author: DW Documentary
item.content:encoded:
How do we break free from a spiral of hate? This documentary follows people in Bosnia, Mexico, and Canada who have found ways to deal with hate—and to overcome it.
As the host of a children’s show, Tobi Krell is surrounded by closeness and trust. At the same time, he observes a growing coarsening of society worldwide: People treat one another with aggression, violence, and hostile stereotypes. He sets out to look for approaches to breaking the cycle of hate. In Sarajevo, he meets Adnan, a war veteran. Three decades after the end of the Bosnian War, tensions remain palpable. Adnan grapples with the question of how to dispel stereotypes—and what it takes to counter them in everyday life. In Canada, Tobi Krell meets Lauren and her mother. As a teenager, Lauren joined a far-right group. The two explain how they were able to stay in touch despite this experience—and what role personal bonds play in leaving such groups. In Monterrey, in northeastern Mexico, Anni shares her experiences with domestic violence. She shows how she has learned to reflect on her own upbringing and find new ways of dealing with conflicts. The documentary asks: How does hatred arise—and how can we overcome it? Three examples open up three different perspectives.

item.title: How China Plans to Win the Global AI Race
item.author: Bloomberg Originals
item.content:encoded:
China’s low-cost, open-weight artificial intelligence models are rapidly gaining ground on US rivals such as OpenAI and Anthropic. In June, global usage of Chinese AI models surpassed US models for the first time, according to OpenRouter data.
From DeepSeek to Kimi K3, Chinese AI companies are attracting users around the world, including in Silicon Valley, where hundreds of startup founders urged the Trump administration not to restrict access to Chinese AI models.
The shift comes as concerns grow over the risks of advanced AI, with company CEOs including Dario Amodei of Anthropic and Sam Altman of OpenAI calling for stronger safeguards and slower development.

item.title: Everything you need to know about bird flu - Benjamin Anderson
item.author: TED-Ed
item.content:encoded:
Dig into the science of avian influenza to find out what makes the H5N1 virus so dangerous, and its potential to jump to humans.
--
While avian influenza used to infect mostly birds, in the past few years, it’s been found in over 70 mammal species, including cats, dairy cows, foxes, seals, and bears. Each new mammalian infection gives the virus more chances to drift or shift, spill over into humans, and ignite a pandemic. So, what is it about H5N1 that makes it so frighteningly flexible? Benjamin Anderson investigates.

item.title: Eco-burial - Would you consider being composted? | DW Documentary
item.author: DW Documentary
item.content:encoded:
An increasing number of people don't want to be cremated or buried after their death. They want their bodies to return to the earth as fertile soil. This poses both an ethical and a legal challenge.
In Europe, committed citizens are campaigning to have 'humusation' - the composting of human remains - scientifically investigated, validated and legalized. In the US, this alternative to cremation and burial is already practiced in two states. The idea is culturally radical but based on a natural process. Called ‘aerobic decomposition,’ it has been perfected by nature over millions of years.
Gradually, a movement is emerging that was long regarded as marginal and controversial. Its pioneers are breaking taboos, raising environmental awareness and challenging the funeral industry. Through what's known as 're-burial', they're shaping a different understanding of death - as part of a cycle that renews life - thereby paving the way for new rites.

item.content:encoded:
How record-breaking distance runner Lornah Kiplagat helped other women in Kenya break social barriers and train to be professional runners. (Aired March 2004)
This journalism is made possible by viewers like you. Donate to FRONTLINE now: https://bit.ly/47DFzCb
And support your local PBS station here: https://www.pbs.org/donate
For decades, Kenyan men had ranked among the world’s best long distance runners — bringing home one Olympic medal after another and sweeping marathons from coast to coast in the U.S. Largely confined to traditional roles at home and on the farm, most Kenyan women had only watched from the sidelines. But when Lornah Kiplagat emerged from the highlands of northwest Kenya as one of the best female runners in the world in the late 1990s and early 2000s, she committed herself and her prize money to building what was then the first women’s running camp in the country.
In “Kenya: Run, Lornah, Run,” FRONTLINE/World correspondents Alexis Bloom and Cassandra Herrman documented Kiplagat’s journey, met emerging female athletes at her unique camp, and learned about how they were breaking social expectations in a country that largely prescribed traditional, domestic roles for women. As Kiplagat noted in the documentary, “At the end, it’s not only about running. It’s a way of changing the whole lifestyle of women in Kenya.”
In the two decades since “Run, Lornah, Run” aired, Kiplagat’s camp, the High Altitude Training Center, has become a destination for elite runners — both female and male — from around the world. Kiplagat, now a citizen of the Netherlands, continues to support young women in Kenya through programming at the center and through her eponymous foundation.
“Kenya: Run, Lornah, Run” was produced and reported by Alexis Bloom and Cassandra Herrman. The founder and executive producer of FRONTLINE was David Fanning.
